newsitem.title: USA: Lear agrees to buy Goodyear instrument panel unit.
newsitem.headline: Lear agrees to buy Goodyear instrument panel unit.

text.p: Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. said Tuesday it has agreed to sell its Logan, Ohio, instrument panel and trim plant to automotive interior supplier Lear Corp. for an undisclosed sum.
The deal will boost Lear's capacity to design and manufacture car and truck instrument panels, helping to round out the Southfield, Mich.-based company's product offerings.

The plant, which employs 624 people, will become Lear's first North American instrument panel plant and will complement Lear's $85 million acquisition of Swedish instrument panel maker Borealis Industrier AB in December.
Goodyear spokesman David Wilkins declined to disclose the price, but said the deal will allow Akron, Ohio-based Goodyear to focus on its tire, moulded rubber and other core businesses.
A Lear representative was not available to comment on the transaction.

The Goodyear factory, 50 miles southeast of Columbus, Ohio, is not affected by a United Steelworkers of America strike at 10 other Goodyear plants in Ohio, Alabama, Nebraska, North Carolina Kansas, Tennessee, Virginia and Wisconsin. Employees are represented under a separate agreement with the Steelworkers union.
The plant's biggest production contracts include panels for Ford Motor Co.'s Ford Taurus and Mercury Sable cars and General Motors Corp.'s new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass sedans.

Michael Robinet, an analyst with CSM Forecasting Inc. in Farmington Hills, Mich., said the sale of Goodyear's instrument panel business represents another step in the massive consolidation of the automotive interiors industry.

In the past two years, Lear and its chief competitors, Johnson Controls Inc. and Magna International Inc. MG.TO, have bought up smaller makers of seats, door panels, carpeting and other components in an effort to be able to offer complete vehicle interior packages to automakers.
"With each of the three integrators, they're going to beef up whatever capability is not strong now," Robinet said.
Separately, Lear said Tuesday that acquisitions and a favourable sales mix helped it boost first-quarter earnings by 62.4 percent to a record $41.9 million.
Lear said its net income for the quarter ended March 29, equal to 62 cents a share, compared with year-earlier earnings of $25.8 million, or 43 cents a share.

Lear's revenues for the first quarter increased to $1.7 billion from $1.4 billion a year earlier. About $47.7 million of the increase was attributable to the Borealis acquisition, while Lear gained $159 million in increased revenues from its acquisition of carpet maker Masland Industries Inc.
